examples.japanese: {蚊|か}は{吸血|きゅうけつ}する{昆虫|こんちゅう}です。
{吸血|きゅうけつ}コウモリは{中南米|ちゅうなんべい}に{生息|せいそく}する。
examples.english: Vampire bats inhabit Central and South America.

examples.japanese: ダニに{吸血|きゅうけつ}されると、{感染症|かんせんしょう}のリスクがあるので{注意|ちゅうい}が{必要|ひつよう}だ。
examples.english: Being bitten by a tick carries a risk of infection, so caution is necessary.

notes:
Literally "sucking blood" — a compound of {吸|きゅう} (to suck/inhale) + {血|けつ} (blood). Used both for the literal biological act (mosquitoes, ticks, leeches) and in the context of vampire fiction.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {吸血|きゅうけつ}{鬼|き}: vampire (literally "blood-sucking demon")
- {吸血|きゅうけつ}コウモリ: vampire bat
- {吸血|きゅうけつ}{行為|こうい}: act of blood-sucking
- {吸血|きゅうけつ}{昆虫|こんちゅう}: blood-sucking insect

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {吸血鬼|きゅうけつき}: vampire (the creature itself; most common compound)
- {採血|さいけつ}: drawing blood (medical procedure; neutral/clinical term)
- {輸血|ゆけつ}: blood transfusion (medical procedure of transferring blood)

USAGE:
In everyday Japanese, {吸血|きゅうけつ} appears most often as a modifier in compounds like {吸血鬼|きゅうけつき} (vampire). The verb form {吸血|きゅうけつ}する is used mainly in scientific or nature documentary contexts to describe how animals feed on blood.
